title: Things to do in Savannah: 5 places from squares to the river
description: Explore five Savannah places: Forsyth Park, Chippewa Square, the cathedral, River Street and Bonaventure, with a practical route and visiting advice.
relatedQueries: places to visit in Savannah Georgia
intro: For a first visit to Savannah, choose five places with different roles: Forsyth Park for green space, Chippewa Square for the city’s squares, the Cathedral Basilica of St. John the Baptist for a working religious building, River Street for the waterfront and Bonaventure for a heritage visit beyond the central walk. This guide covers Savannah, Georgia, in the United States, and helps you decide how each stop fits your trip.

The first four places can be organised within a central urban itinerary, allowing for breaks and the interiors you actually want to visit. Bonaventure needs a separate block and its own transport plan; it is not another square along the same street. The photographs are documentary archive images with their years identified. They help you recognise places, while opening arrangements and access should be checked for your travel dates.

sections.heading: 1. Forsyth Park: look beyond the fountain
paragraphs: The white fountain at the northern end gives you an obvious starting point. The city dates its installation to 1858 and explains that the park expanded from an original ten-acre plot to its present thirty acres. That size matters when planning: photographing the fountain is not the same as exploring Forsyth. Beyond the familiar landmark are walking paths, green space, sports facilities and monuments that also form part of everyday life for residents.

Arrive with a simple decision in mind: which part of the park do you want to enjoy, and where will you go next? If you are continuing towards the central squares, the northern connection helps avoid crossing the grounds again unnecessarily. If you want a break, allow time to walk and sit rather than treating the stop as a single photograph. The municipal page brings together conservation and project updates; check it if a particular facility is essential to your plans.

This guide’s fountain photograph was taken in 2015. It does not establish today’s water operation, planting or access arrangements. Distinguishing archive imagery from practical information helps you avoid organising your visit around a detail that may be under maintenance.

sections.heading: 2. Chippewa Square: understand the city through one square
paragraphs: Chippewa lets you examine one of the spaces that organise a walk through Savannah. Visit Savannah’s official itinerary dates its design to 1815 and connects its name with the Battle of Chippewa during the War of 1812. A bronze statue of James Edward Oglethorpe stands in the centre. Look at how paths, planting and surrounding buildings relate before heading elsewhere; the point is to understand this particular square rather than count every corner as another attraction.

The Forrest Gump connection comes with a useful correction. The bus-stop scenes were filmed on the northern side, but the famous bench does not remain there. The tourist office says it is in a museum. Come to recognise the urban setting rather than expecting a film prop to be permanently installed. The accompanying photograph focuses on the statue among trees; it does not show the entire square layout.

Chippewa works as a pause between the waterfront and the park. Identify your next destination before crossing the surrounding streets, and keep entrances clear as you take photographs. A stop at a nearby business is an additional decision, with its own opening arrangements, rather than something included in a public-square visit.

sections.heading: 3. Cathedral Basilica: visit a working place of worship
paragraphs: The towers and rose window of the Cathedral Basilica of St. John the Baptist offer a different architectural experience from the square and park. The institution emphasises that it is an active Catholic church. Tourism can coexist with religious life, but does not take priority over it: funerals, weddings and other religious events can suspend touring. Treat the exterior as the dependable point of recognition within your walk, and plan an interior visit only after checking the calendar.

The official website states that it does not sell tickets for visits. A voluntary donation should not be confused with an admission ticket sold by an intermediary. Groups must give advance notice even if they do not need a docent. The church also identifies an elevator on Harris Street. If that entrance matters for your mobility, confirm its availability and access instructions before arriving instead of assuming all doors provide the same route.

When the source was checked, it carried a touring-closure notice for Thanksgiving on November 26. That illustrates why holiday announcements matter alongside regular hours. The 2016 archive photograph documents the facade, not a current ceremony. Professional photography and video shoots require advance permission; an ordinary leisure visit does not automatically authorise a commercial production.

sections.heading: 4. River Street: connect the waterfront with its history
paragraphs: River Street connects the present-day walk with buildings formerly used as cotton warehouses. Visit Savannah describes that earlier use, while its walking itinerary links the lower waterfront with Bay Street through stairs, ramps and other access points. Decide how you will get back up before descending. Stone surfaces and changes in level call for particular care if you have a stroller, luggage or a need to avoid steps. Use a map to choose an entrance, not simply locate the river.

Leave time to look across the Savannah River and compare the former industrial facades. This stop does not require a cruise to make sense; boat trips, meals and shopping are separate activities with their own arrangements. The 2023 photograph shows building fronts and paving, so it does not certify that the pictured businesses still occupy the same premises.

The waterfront’s history also deserves attention beyond its commercial appearance. The official Black heritage itinerary describes the African American Family Monument on River Street as a newly emancipated family, with broken chains symbolising a new beginning. Use that interpretation to approach the history of slavery and African American communities with context, rather than treating warehouses and memorials only as an attractive setting.

sections.heading: 5. Bonaventure Cemetery: allow a separate, respectful outing
paragraphs: Bonaventure lies east of Savannah on a bluff above the Wilmington River. The city gives its entrance as 330 Bonaventure Road and explains that the former plantation property became a private cemetery in 1846 and a public cemetery in 1907. Its grounds cover more than one hundred acres, and the tree-lined roads justify a dedicated block of time. The 2024 photograph shows a broad landscape of path, planting and gravestones; it is not a funeral photograph or permission to enter any burial plot.

Plan your outward and return journeys before adding Bonaventure to the itinerary. On arrival, use the authorised gates and cemetery map, and choose a route you can walk comfortably. Municipal rules prohibit remaining after visiting hours without specific permission. For a first visit, a smaller, considered route is more useful than hunting for familiar names without understanding how the sections are arranged.

This remains a place of burial and mourning. Rules prohibit intruding on funeral parties, lingering around an open grave, loud conversation, and sitting or leaning on monuments. If a service is taking place, leave the immediate area and respect the quiet. Do not remove objects or turn the visit into a treasure hunt: appreciating its heritage depends on caring for the people and the place.

sections.heading: Organise the five visits without forcing them into one route
paragraphs: For central Savannah, you can reverse the official route linking River Street with Forsyth Park. Choose whether to begin or finish by the water around the cathedral calendar and your breaks. Chippewa gives you a pause along the way; the church requires a small, planned detour. Walking times published for somebody else’s route are not a promise for your group: crossings, stops and interior visits change the pace.

Save the addresses and check the forecast before leaving. Along the riverfront, examine ramps and stairs; for the church, confirm the Harris Street entrance if needed; at Bonaventure, establish how you will enter and return. Keep transport, meals, booked visits and shopping as separate budget categories. Recognising public exteriors does not make commercial services or guided tours part of an included package.

sections.heading: Choose where to spend longer
paragraphs: If urban landscapes interest you, leave more time for Forsyth’s paths and Chippewa’s setting. For history, connect the River Street warehouses with the Black heritage interpretation rather than expecting facades alone to explain the lives of those who worked there. If religious architecture is your priority, build the central part of your day around a confirmed church visit while keeping an exterior alternative.

The Greenville, New Orleans and Washington, D.C. guides offer other ways to plan United States cities. They are independent stages of a wider trip, not nearby excursions from Savannah. Compare intercity travel arrangements before combining bookings. This guide aims to make five Savannah places understandable, without adding distant destinations to increase the count.

itinerary: First day: begin at Forsyth Park’s northern end and continue towards Chippewa, or reverse the direction. Include the cathedral only within a confirmed visiting period; if worship or a closure takes priority, appreciate the exterior without interrupting religious activity.

Keep another block for River Street, identifying the connection between the waterfront and Bay Street in advance. Allow time to rest and observe the buildings and river without depending on a cruise or restaurant booking.

Use a second day or a separate block for Bonaventure, with municipal visiting arrangements and your return journey organised. Choose a route proportionate to your time and mobility, and remain clear of any funeral service.

faq.question: Can I see all five Savannah places in one day?
faq.answer: You can recognise much of the central area in a day, but Bonaventure has a different location and needs its own transport and time. Separating the central walk from the cemetery helps avoid hurried transfers and interior visits.

faq.question: Is the Forrest Gump bench still in Chippewa Square?
faq.answer: No. Visit Savannah says the bench is in a museum. You can recognise the setting of the scenes filmed on the northern side without expecting the prop to remain installed in the square.

faq.question: Do I need to buy a ticket for the cathedral?
faq.answer: The institution states that it does not sell visiting tickets. Check its calendar because religious events and holiday notices can suspend touring. A donation, an external guided tour and entry to the church are different arrangements.

faq.question: Which Bonaventure Cemetery rules matter for visitors?
faq.answer: Use the authorised gates, keep within visiting hours and stay quiet and clear of funerals. Municipal rules prohibit intruding on funeral parties, leaning on monuments and removing objects. Consult the map and plan your return before starting.

conclusion: Savannah becomes clearer when these five visits connect: the park and square reveal everyday public spaces, the cathedral retains its religious purpose, River Street links commerce and memory, and Bonaventure calls for a different pace and respect. Decide what you want to understand at each stop, check the access arrangements that shape your route and leave time to look. The result is a more meaningful visit than simply collecting familiar photographs.
